prompt: What is requirements discovery, according to the course text?

options.text: The process and techniques analysts use to identify and extract system problems and solution requirements from the user community
The process of turning off the old system
Writing the program code from the requirements

explanation: Requirements discovery pulls problems and requirements out of the user community, working together with users.

why.a: Correct. That is the text's definition.
why.b: Wrong. That is installation.
why.c: Wrong. Coding is implementation.
why.d: Wrong. Deployment diagrams are Module Three UML.

prompt: How does the course text define a PROBLEM?

options.text: An undesirable situation that prevents the organisation from fully achieving its mission, vision, goals and objectives
A requirement the users have not yet stated
A change requested during the support phase

explanation: A problem stands between the organisation and its mission, vision, goals and objectives.

why.a: Wrong. A bug is narrower than the text's definition.
why.b: Correct. The text's definition, word for word in substance.
why.c: Wrong. An unstated requirement is not how the text defines a problem.
why.d: Wrong. That is maintenance or enhancement.

prompt: True or false: requirements discovery requires analytical, communication and interpersonal skills, including resolving conflicting requirements and validating findings with stakeholders.
explanation: Listen carefully, ask the right questions, resolve conflicts, and validate findings for accuracy and completeness.

why.true: Correct. The text names all of these.
why.false: Wrong. The text lists exactly these skills and duties.

prompt: The process of requirements discovery consists of four activities. Which list is correct?

options.text: Problem discovery and analysis, requirements discovery, documenting and analysing requirements, requirements management

explanation: Discover and analyse the problem, discover the requirements, document and analyse them, then manage them.

why.a: Wrong. Those are SDLC phases.
why.b: Correct. The four activities.
why.c: Wrong. Those are fact-finding techniques, used within discovery.
why.d: Wrong. Those resemble project planning activities.

prompt: Match each term with its meaning in the course text.

pairs.right: What the information system must DO
What the information system must HAVE
An undesirable situation preventing the organisation from achieving its goals

explanation: Two types of requirement come out of discovery: functional, what the system must do, and non-functional, what it must have. Together, system requirements, also called business requirements.

prompt: Which two types of requirements are identified during requirements discovery?
explanation: Functional (what it must do) and non-functional (what it must have).

why.a: Wrong. Logical and physical describe models, not requirement types.
why.b: Wrong. Not the text's types.
why.c: Correct. Functional and non-functional.
why.d: Wrong. Structured and unstructured are types of INTERVIEW.

prompt: True or false: facilitated workshops, also called Joint Application Development sessions, are among the common fact-gathering techniques used in requirements discovery.
explanation: Common techniques: interviews, questionnaires, observation, document analysis, facilitated workshops or JAD sessions, and sometimes prototyping.

why.true: Correct. Facilitated workshops are on the list.

prompt: According to the course text, system requirements serve as what between stakeholders and the development team?
explanation: System requirements state what the system should do and the conditions it must operate under, and they serve as a formal agreement between stakeholders and developers.

why.a: Correct. A formal agreement.
why.b: Wrong. Test plans are a design deliverable.
why.c: Wrong. A deployment diagram is a UML model.
why.d: Wrong. The text calls them formal, not informal.

prompt: During which SDLC phase are system requirements developed?
explanation: Analysis. They then provide the basis for design, implementation, testing and evaluation.

why.a: Wrong. Planning defines scope and feasibility.
why.b: Correct. Requirements are developed in analysis.
why.c: Wrong. By implementation the requirements are already used.
why.d: Wrong. Support follows installation.

prompt: Which two of these are among the six results of incorrect requirements in the course text?

options.text: The system may cost more than projected
The system will be finished early
The reputation of the IT staff is tarnished

explanation: The six: over cost; late; not meeting expectations, so unused; excessive maintenance cost; unreliable; and the IT staff's reputation tarnished.

why.a: Correct. Cost overrun is one of the six.
why.b: Wrong. Incorrect requirements make it LATER, not earlier.
why.c: Correct. Tarnished reputation is one of the six.
why.d: Wrong. The text says maintenance costs may be excessively HIGH.

prompt: True or false: one result of incorrect requirements is that the system may be unreliable, prone to errors and downtime.
explanation: Unreliability is one of the six results.

why.true: Correct. It is on the list.
why.false: Wrong. It is one of the six results.

prompt: The formal process of using research, meetings, interviews, questionnaires, sampling and other techniques to collect information about system problems, requirements and preferences is called:
explanation: Fact-finding, also called information gathering or data collection.

why.a: Correct. Fact-finding.
why.b: Wrong. Decomposition breaks a system into sub-processes.
why.c: Wrong. Balancing keeps DFD levels consistent.
why.d: Wrong. Encapsulation is an object-oriented concept.

prompt: Which two other names does the course text give fact-finding?
explanation: Fact-finding is also called information gathering or data collection.

why.a: Correct. Information gathering.
why.b: Wrong. That is dividing a system into subsystems.
why.c: Correct. Data collection.
why.d: Wrong. That is the fourth activity of requirements discovery.

prompt: Fact-finding brings the analyst into contact with sensitive information. What are the analyst's two ethical duties towards it?

options.text: To publish it so users trust the project
To protect it from people who would misuse it
To delete it as soon as it is seen

explanation: Two duties: do not misuse it, and protect it from those who would. The information includes company plans, salaries, medical history, and customer credit card or social security details.

why.a: Correct. Do not misuse it.
why.b: Wrong. Publishing sensitive data is a breach.
why.c: Correct. Protect it from misuse.
why.d: Wrong. The duty is to protect it, not to destroy it.

prompt: True or false: the course text gives employee salaries and medical history as examples of sensitive information met during fact-finding.
explanation: Company plans, employee salaries or medical history, and customer credit card or social security information.

prompt: Which of these is NOT a consequence of breaching fact-finding ethics in the course text?

options.text: The analyst loses the respect, credibility and confidence of users and management
The organisation and analyst could have legal liability
The analyst could lose a job

explanation: The three consequences: loss of respect and credibility, legal liability, and possibly the loss of a job.

why.a: Wrong choice, because this IS a consequence.
why.b: Wrong choice, because this IS a consequence.
why.c: Wrong choice, because this IS a consequence.
why.d: Correct. A breach brings no approval; it harms the analyst and the organisation.

prompt: The course text says the Requirements Definition Document serves as what for the system's project?
explanation: It communicates the requirements to key stakeholders and serves as a CONTRACT, describing functions and constraints at a high level in business language.

why.a: Correct. A contract.
why.b: Wrong. Not the text's description.
why.c: Wrong. A user manual is training material, in implementation.
why.d: Wrong. A prototype is a model, not a document.

prompt: Match each tool for documenting draft requirements with its description.

pairs.right: How actors interact with the system to achieve goals, from the user's perspective
Complex business rules, listing all conditions and their actions
Requirements organised with an ID, description, type, source, priority and status

explanation: Three documentation tools. Use cases for interactions, decision tables for complex rules, requirements tables for an organised list.

prompt: A business rule depends on several conditions, each combination leading to a different action. Which documentation tool does the course text provide for this?
explanation: Decision tables represent complex business rules by listing all conditions and the corresponding actions.

why.a: Wrong. A requirements table lists requirements with ID, type, source, priority and status.
why.b: Correct. A decision table.
why.c: Wrong. A use case describes actor interactions.
why.d: Wrong. A context diagram is a DFD level, not a documentation tool for rules.

prompt: Which two of these are other names the course text gives the requirements definition document?
explanation: Also called the requirements definition report, requirements statement, requirements specification, or functional specifications.

why.a: Correct. Requirements specification.
why.b: Wrong. Not one of the names given.
why.c: Correct. Functional specifications.
why.d: Wrong. Maintenance reports are a support deliverable.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the SEVEN fact-finding techniques in the course text?
explanation: The seven: sampling documentation, forms and databases; research and site visits; observation; questionnaires; interviews; prototyping; joint requirements planning.

why.a: Wrong choice, because this IS one of the seven.
why.b: Wrong choice, because this IS one of the seven.
why.c: Correct. Functional decomposition divides a system into subsystems; it is not a fact-finding technique.
why.d: Wrong choice, because this IS one of the seven.

prompt: True or false: the course text lists SEVEN fact-finding techniques.
explanation: Seven: sampling, research and site visits, observation, questionnaires, interviews, prototyping, and JRP.

why.true: Correct. The text lists seven techniques.

prompt: When sampling existing documentation, which two of these does the course text say the analyst reviews?
explanation: The organisation chart, memos describing the problem, standard operating procedures, completed forms, screens and reports, database samples, flowcharts and system documentation.

why.a: Correct. The organisation chart is reviewed.
why.b: Wrong. Not in the list, and not the organisation's documentation.
why.c: Correct. Completed forms are reviewed.
why.d: Wrong. Not the organisation's own documentation, and an ethical breach.

prompt: True or false: sampling existing documents helps identify redundancies and inconsistencies in processes and recordkeeping, as well as data quality issues.
explanation: It gives insight into processes, business rules and information requirements, and exposes redundancies, inconsistencies and data quality problems.

why.true: Correct. The text says exactly this.
why.false: Wrong. The text names these benefits.

prompt: Which fact-finding technique uncovers informal procedures, workarounds and bottlenecks that users may not mention in interviews?
explanation: Observation: the analyst participates in or watches the work, and so sees what people do rather than what they say they do.

why.a: Wrong. Questionnaires only capture what respondents choose to write.
why.b: Correct. Observation gives first-hand understanding.
why.c: Wrong. Documents record the official procedure, not the informal one.
why.d: Wrong. Brainstorming generates ideas.

prompt: Which of these goes AGAINST the course text's observation guidelines?

options.text: Obtaining permission from supervisors or managers
Informing those observed of the purpose
Interrupting the individuals at work to ask questions
Reviewing observation notes with appropriate individuals

explanation: The guidelines say do NOT interrupt the individuals at work. Also: plan the who, what, where, when, why and how; keep a low profile; take notes; do not focus on trivia; do not assume.

why.a: Wrong choice, because obtaining permission IS a guideline.
why.b: Wrong choice, because informing people IS a guideline.
why.c: Correct. Interrupting is exactly what the guidelines forbid.
why.d: Wrong choice, because reviewing notes IS a guideline.

prompt: True or false: the observation guidelines tell the analyst to keep a low profile and not to make assumptions.
explanation: Both are among the nine guidelines.

why.false: Wrong. Both appear in the nine guidelines.

prompt: Match each term with its description in the course text.

pairs.right: A special-purpose document to collect information and opinions from many respondents quickly and cheaply
Gives the respondent latitude, with the answer written in the space provided
Requires selecting an answer from predefined responses
Types of fixed-format question, with multiple-choice

explanation: Questionnaires reach many people cheaply. Free-format lets them write; fixed-format makes them choose, with multiple-choice, rating and ranking questions.

prompt: Information is needed from many people, quickly and at low cost. Which technique does the course text say is useful here?
explanation: Questionnaires collect information and opinions from many respondents quickly and cheaply.

why.a: Correct. A questionnaire.
why.b: Wrong. Interviews are face to face, one at a time.
why.c: Wrong. Observation watches individuals at work.
why.d: Wrong. JRP sessions are costly structured meetings.

prompt: The course text lists what interviews can be used for. Which two are on that list?
explanation: Interviews can find, verify and clarify facts, generate enthusiasm, involve the end-user, identify requirements, and solicit ideas and opinions.

why.a: Correct. Verifying facts is a use.
why.b: Wrong. Installation is an implementation activity.
why.c: Correct. Generating enthusiasm is a use.
why.d: Wrong. Data conversion is an implementation activity.

prompt: Match each interview term with its meaning.

pairs.right: A general goal and few specific questions; the interviewee directs the conversation
The interviewer has a specific set of questions to ask
The interviewee may respond in any way that seems appropriate
Answers restricted to specific choices or short direct responses

explanation: Structure is about the INTERVIEW, planned or not; openness is about each QUESTION, free or restricted.

prompt: An analyst goes in with only a general subject in mind and lets the interviewee direct the conversation. What kind of interview is this?
explanation: Unstructured: a general goal, few if any specific questions, and the interviewee provides the framework.

why.a: Wrong. A structured interview has a specific set of questions.
why.b: Correct. Unstructured.
why.c: Wrong. Closed-ended describes a kind of question, not a kind of interview.
why.d: Wrong. JRP is a structured group meeting.

prompt: What does the course text call the checklist of specific questions used to prepare for an interview?
explanation: The interview guide. The procedure: define the objective, select interviewees, prepare with the guide, conduct, follow up.

why.a: Correct. An interview guide.
why.b: Wrong. Decision tables document business rules.
why.c: Wrong. Requirements tables organise requirements.
why.d: Wrong. An agenda is prepared for a JRP session.

prompt: True or false: the interview procedure has five stages, beginning with defining the objective of the interview and ending with following up on it.
explanation: Define the objective, select interviewees, prepare, conduct, follow up.

why.true: Correct. Five stages, in that order.
why.false: Wrong. That is the text's procedure.

prompt: What does the course text mean by BODY LANGUAGE in its interview guidelines?

options.text: The formal wording of the questions
The non-verbal information we communicate, including facial disclosure, eye contact and posture
The notes taken by the scribe
The technical jargon of the IT staff

explanation: Body language is non-verbal communication, and the guidelines tell the analyst to attend to it, along with a positive attitude, putting the person at ease, listening, asking questions, not assuming, and taking notes.

why.a: Wrong. That is verbal.
why.b: Correct. Non-verbal information: face, eyes, posture.
why.c: Wrong. Scribes belong to JRP.
why.d: Wrong. Jargon is to be avoided, and it is verbal.

prompt: True or false: following up on an interview means validating the documented responses with the interviewee or stakeholders, to ensure correctness and avoid misunderstandings.
explanation: Follow-up improves the reliability of the gathered information.

why.false: Wrong. The text defines follow-up exactly so.

prompt: Building a small-scale, representative or working model of the users' requirements to discover or verify them is called:
explanation: Discovery prototyping is particularly useful when requirements are unclear or the user interface is critical.

why.a: Correct. Discovery prototyping.
why.b: Wrong. Pilot conversion gives a new system to a small group of users.
why.c: Wrong. Decomposition breaks processes down.
why.d: Wrong. Sampling reviews existing documents.

prompt: True or false: discovery prototyping is particularly useful when requirements are unclear or when user interface design is critical to success.
explanation: Both situations are named: users react to a model better than to a description.

why.false: Wrong. The text names both situations.

prompt: How does the course text relate JRP to Joint Application Development?

options.text: JRP is a subset of JAD, which covers the entire systems development process
JAD is a subset of JRP
JRP replaces JAD in modern projects

explanation: JRP, structured group meetings to analyse problems and define requirements, is a SUBSET of JAD, which encompasses the whole development process.

why.a: Correct. JRP is a subset of JAD.
why.b: Wrong. This reverses the relationship.
why.c: Wrong. The text explicitly relates them.
why.d: Wrong. The text says nothing of replacement.

prompt: Which two of these are JRP participants in the course text?
explanation: The participants: the sponsor, the facilitator, users and managers, scribes, and IT staff.

why.a: Correct. The facilitator runs the session.
why.b: Wrong. Not participants.
why.c: Correct. Scribes take notes.
why.d: Wrong. Not in the list.

prompt: What are the three steps to plan a JRP session?

options.text: Select a location, select the participants, prepare the agenda
Define the objective, conduct, follow up

explanation: Location (away from the workplace if possible, well equipped), participants (released from regular duties), and an agenda with briefing documents sent beforehand.

why.a: Correct. Location, participants, agenda.
why.b: Wrong. That resembles the interview procedure.
why.c: Wrong. Those are fact-finding techniques.
why.d: Wrong. That is the evolutionary prototyping loop.

prompt: True or false: the course text recommends holding a JRP session away from the workplace when possible.
explanation: Away from the workplace, in several equipped rooms, with participants released from their regular duties.

why.true: Correct. Away from the workplace when possible.
why.false: Wrong. The text recommends exactly this.

prompt: Which of these goes AGAINST the guidelines for a successful JRP session?

options.text: Let one confident individual dominate the discussion

explanation: Encourage participation WITHOUT allowing individuals to dominate. Also: keep to the agenda, stay on schedule, let the scribe take notes, avoid jargon, resolve conflict, allow breaks, seek consensus, keep the ground rules.

why.a: Wrong choice, because staying on schedule IS a guideline.
why.b: Wrong choice, because ample breaks ARE a guideline.
why.c: Correct. The guidelines forbid letting individuals dominate.
why.d: Wrong choice, because avoiding jargon IS a guideline.

prompt: What is the defining rule of brainstorming in the course text?

options.text: Each idea is analysed as soon as it is offered
As many ideas as possible in a short time, with NO analysis until all ideas are exhausted
Ideas are submitted anonymously by questionnaire

explanation: Quantity first, judgement later. Brainstorming is the common way a JRP session generates possible solutions.

why.a: Wrong. Analysing each idea at once is exactly what brainstorming forbids.
why.b: Correct. No analysis until the ideas run out.
why.c: Wrong. Everyone calls out ideas.
why.d: Wrong. Ideas are called out aloud and recorded.

prompt: True or false: the brainstorming guidelines say to appoint one person to record the ideas, and to analyse and evaluate them only after the group has run out of ideas.
explanation: One recorder, ideas called out fast, evaluation only at the end, then refine, combine and improve.

why.false: Wrong. Both are in the text's guidelines.

prompt: Which two of these are among the three benefits of JRP?

options.text: It actively involves users and management, encouraging ownership
It removes the need for any documentation
It reduces the time required to develop systems
It guarantees there will be no conflict

explanation: The three: involvement and ownership; less development time; and, when JRP uses prototyping to confirm requirements, the benefits of prototyping.

why.a: Correct. Involvement and ownership.
why.b: Wrong. Scribes document everything.
why.c: Correct. Reduced development time.
why.d: Wrong. The guidelines call for conflict resolution skills, so conflict is expected.

prompt: Match each situation with the fact-finding technique it describes.

pairs.left: Watching a clerk process orders for a morning
A face-to-face conversation with the payroll manager
Reading the standard operating procedures and completed forms
Structured group meetings of sponsor, users, managers and IT staff

explanation: Watching is observation; face to face with one person is an interview; reading documents is sampling; the structured group meeting is JRP.
